description: Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware across the solar system–on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. From rovers and instruments that completed their science missions to probes still traveling away from Earth this hardware varies widely in both its purpose and current level of functionality. Your challenge is to tell the story of some or all of this equipment that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the hardware and the science it made possible.
summary:
Stellar Narrators is an interactive website where NASA's forgotten space equipment finally gets to tell its own story. Guided by Nova, a friendly astronaut, students explore hardware left behind across different worlds, starting with the Apollo 11 Lunar Module "Eagle" and its science instruments, as well as Mars exploration machines like Ingenuity, Sojourner, and InSight.

We built it for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge. Using NASA's open data and open-source scripts, we turned facts about each machine into short stories. Nova walks kids through what every piece of equipment did, how it worked, and what happened to it after the mission ended.

We think this matters because space history can feel distant and boring to young learners. When a piece of space equipment "speaks" for itself, kids connect with it, get curious about science, and remember that these missions still deserve to be remembered.
details:
Stellar Narrators is an interactive website where NASA's abandoned space equipment finally gets to tell its own story. Nova, a friendly astronaut guide, takes students on a tour of hardware left behind across different worlds, starting with the Apollo 11 Lunar Module "Eagle" and its science instruments, then exploring Mars missions like Ingenuity, Sojourner, and InSight. Kids can click through each piece of equipment to discover what it did, how it worked, and what happened to it after the mission ended. Everything is told as a short story, not a boring list of facts.

We built it because space history can feel far away from young learners, and we wanted to change that. When the equipment itself becomes the storyteller, students can explore real NASA missions without needing any science background. We hope kids walk away curious about space and remember that even machines that stopped working long ago helped science move forward.

Every space mission has a story, but what happens when a rover stops moving, a lander loses contact with Earth, or a spacecraft completes its final mission? These machines may become silent, but their discoveries and contributions remain part of humanity's journey through space.

Our website allows visitors to explore these missions through immersive visuals, interactive experiences, and engaging stories. Each mission has its own dedicated section, revealing its purpose, achievements, final moments, and lasting legacy.

Guiding visitors through this journey is NOVA, our original space companion, who adds personality, curiosity, and a sense of adventure to the experience. NOVA helps make space exploration feel more personal and accessible, especially for younger audiences.

Rather than simply presenting scientific facts, Forgotten, Not Gone invites visitors to connect with the stories behind the machines and discover why even abandoned equipment still matters.

Our mission is to preserve the legacy of these silent explorers, inspire curiosity about space, and remind people that every mission leaves something valuable behind.

Forgotten, Not Gone — Their missions ended. Their stories didn't.

To make it, we used JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, CSS, React, and Next.js. We developed the project in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/AmrAhmed2009/forgotten-not-gone) and used NASA data and resources, including the NSSDCA archive for the Apollo 11 Lunar Module and EASEP, along with NASA sources about the other missions. We also used AI tools to help us along the way, including improving parts of the content and polishing the project's presentation.

What makes it creative is letting the equipment speak for itself, with Nova guiding kids through the experience like it's an adventure instead of a lesson. While building it, we kept the language simple for school-age students, chose a friendly and easy-to-read design, and made sure the information was based on trusted NASA sources, so the stories are fun but still accurate.
